title: Reported $100,000 OPT Fee Nears Publication, Putting International Students' Work Rights at Risk
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security's proposed "Optional Practical Training Fees" rule has cleared White House review and could soon be published for public comment — attaching a reported six-figure price tag to the post-graduation work program used by hundreds of thousands of foreign graduates each year.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule, titled "Optional Practical Training Fees" (RIN 1653-AB01), was received by the White House regulatory review office on August 20, 2026, and cleared that review on September 11 — the next step is publication in the Federal Register for public comment.
  • Media reports citing sources familiar with the proposal, including The Wall Street Journal, suggest a fee in the range of $100,000 could be attached to OPT participation. The figure has not been confirmed in any official government document.
  • What this means for students right now: nothing changes today. Current OPT and STEM OPT authorizations are unaffected, but a public comment period — and eventually a final rule — could reshape the economics of post-graduation work for students graduating in 2027 and beyond.
  • The rule carries an "Economically Significant" designation, meaning the administration itself expects an annual economic impact of at least $100 million, and it was explicitly flagged for international impacts.

A proposal that could fundamentally reshape how international students work in the United States after graduation has cleared one of its most important procedural hurdles. The Department of Homeland Security formally submitted a proposed rule titled "Optional Practical Training Fees" to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs on August 20, 2026, and OIRA concluded its review on September 11 with the action "Consistent with Change" — meaning the proposal was approved with modifications, according to Bloomberg Law and immigration policy trackers. Federal Register publication, and the public comment period that follows, is now imminent.

What the proposal would change

Optional Practical Training allows F-1 international students to work in the United States in a field directly related to their area of study. Standard OPT provides up to 12 months of work authorization; graduates in science, technology, engineering and mathematics who work in STEM fields can apply for a 24-month STEM OPT extension, for up to three years of post-graduation work.

OPT is the primary bridge between an international student's academic career and the American labor market — how tens of thousands of graduates gain work experience, prove their value to employers, and position themselves for H-1B sponsorship. The program currently carries no separate federal program fee; students pay only the standard Form I-765 USCIS filing fee for their Employment Authorization Document. The proposed rule would change that.

What the fee will actually be remains unconfirmed. The full rule text will become public only when DHS publishes it in the Federal Register. What is confirmed from the official Reginfo.gov filing is the title, its classification as a proposed rule, the August 20 receipt date, and the "Economically Significant" designation — a marker the White House reserves for rules expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more. The filing also explicitly notes international impacts, an acknowledgment that OPT participants come from virtually every country in the world.

Context: the H-1B fee that courts blocked

The OPT proposal does not arrive in a vacuum. Last year, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions for certain employers — a move a federal court blocked in June 2026, ruling it an unlawful fee Congress had never authorized. The First Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston refused to revive the fee on July 24, 2026, and the administration is still appealing. DHS subsequently proposed a new $103,265 fee for H-1B hires through a separate regulatory vehicle.

The OPT proposal appears designed to test whether a different legal vehicle — attaching the fee to a regulatory work-authorization program rather than a visa category — could survive the challenge that sank the H-1B version. The same constitutional arguments that felled the H-1B fee would almost certainly be raised against it.

A broader 2026 tightening of the student pipeline

The fee proposal is the latest in a sustained series of 2026 policy actions targeting the F-1 student pipeline. The duration-of-status rule ended unlimited student visa stays in July. The Student and Exchange Visitor Program issued a warning to universities about improper curricular practical training authorizations in August. New editions of Form I-765 became mandatory in mid-September. OIRA also cleared final rules updating EB-5 investor visa fees and removing automatic extensions of foreign workers' employment authorization documents.

Taken together, the pattern is unmistakable: the federal government is systematically reviewing and tightening every stage of the student visa experience, from admission to practical training to post-graduation work authorization.

Diaspora angle: Indian students in the crosshairs

India sends more students to the United States than any other country — 363,019 in the 2024-25 academic year, out of 1,177,766 international students overall. Roughly 294,000 international students were on OPT in 2024-25, and around 419,000 foreign graduates worked under OPT in 2024, according to immigration reporting citing government data.

For Indian families financing American degrees, the math is brutal. A six-figure fee layered on top of tuition, the existing I-765 filing fee, and living costs would price all but the wealthiest graduates out of the U.S. labor market — and choke the primary talent pipeline for STEM fields and H-1B sponsorships that Silicon Valley and Wall Street rely on. Universities, which depend heavily on international tuition revenue, would feel the contraction too.

What's next

The honest answer for students: watch the Federal Register. When DHS publishes the proposed rule, the full fee amount and the specific terms — who pays, when, and under what circumstances — will become public for the first time. The public comment period that follows is the formal opportunity for students, universities, employers and advocacy groups to get their objections into the administrative record; such comments carry real weight and can reshape a final rule.

Current OPT and STEM OPT authorizations cannot be affected by a proposal still working through rulemaking. But a student graduating in spring 2027 could be filing their OPT application in a very different regulatory environment than the one that exists today — and legal challenges, given the H-1B precedent, are all but certain once publication lands.

nri_angle: With 363,019 Indian students in the US — the largest international student cohort — a six-figure OPT fee would fall hardest on Indian families financing American degrees and the STEM pipeline they feed.
